> **The research decision.** When your answer has to be stitched together from
> several measurements or stages, decide whether the combined design is still one
> aligned thing you can diagnose before you run it. Stacking careful pieces does
> not automatically produce a careful result, and deciding to *cut* a piece you
> cannot characterize is as much a design decision as adding one.

## Why this decision matters

**The decision on the table: whether the extra moving piece in your design earns
its place, or just adds an error you cannot account for.**

> *"Do not hand me the headline number. Hand me the error budget: every quantity you
> measured, how you measured it, and how each one's uncertainty flowed into the final
> answer. A precise result built on one uncharacterized step is a precise wrong
> answer."*
> — an **antitrust economist** reviewing a report that claims to have measured how
> concentrated a market is

A complex design fails in a quiet way. Each piece looks careful on its own, so the whole
looks careful too. But an answer assembled from several measurements is only as
trustworthy as its worst-characterized piece, and the assembly can amplify a small
mistake into a large one. This chapter gives you the discipline to take such a design
apart and diagnose the whole before you trust its number.

## The concept

Every research design has four parts, named **MIDA** by Blair, Cooper, Coppock, and
Humphreys [@blair2019declaring] and developed in RDSS [@blair2023rdss]: the **Model** (your written picture of how the
world could work), the **Inquiry** (the one exact quantity you want from it), the
**Data strategy** (every procedure that makes the data, from sampling to measurement),
and the **Answer strategy** (the whole procedure that turns those data into an answer,
uncertainty included). The Colab lab builds all four from scratch. This chapter takes
them somewhere harder.

A **complex, or hybrid, design** is a research design whose four MIDA parts have more
than one moving piece: several measurements, stages, or sub-questions stitched into a
single answer [@blair2023rdss]. Example: computing a market's concentration score from two separate
measurements, each drawn from its own source and carrying its own error.

Two ideas decide whether such a design holds together. The first is **alignment**,
meaning all four parts point at the same single quantity. Complexity breaks it in a
fresh way: two carefully built sub-measurements can each be fine yet quietly target
slightly different quantities that never combine into the one you named. The second is
**error propagation**, meaning each measured input's uncertainty flows into the final
answer, sometimes amplified [@jcgm2008gum]. Example: if your answer depends on the *square* of a
measured share, a 1% error in that share becomes roughly a 2% error in the result.

Keep the lab's two failure words close. **Bias** is a systematic tilt that more data
does not shrink; **variance** is run-to-run wobble that more data does. Complexity lets
a small systematic error hide behind an impressively small random one.

## A worked example

You want to know how concentrated your city's grocery market is: does a handful of
chains dominate it, or is it split among many sellers? The standard answer is a
**concentration index**, a single score that rises as a market's sales pile up in
fewer hands [@dojftc2023merger]. You compute it by squaring each seller's market share and adding the
squares, where a seller's `share = its revenue / total market revenue`. That one
formula is a complex design in miniature. It stitches two sub-measurements into one
answer: each chain's `revenue`, which you take from a monthly industry survey, and the
`total market revenue` in the denominator, which you have to measure separately.

Watch the anatomy. A single month of reported revenue is noisy, because a holiday week
or a late filing pushes any one chain's figure up or down. So you make a smart
data-strategy move: average twelve months of revenue for each chain before you compute
shares. That averaging crushes the *variance*, and your index looks beautifully
repeatable, moving a point or two at most when you swap which months you use.

Here is the trap the lab trains you to see. Repetition does nothing for *bias*. Your
industry survey covers the chains, but not the independent corner stores or the
online grocery deliveries, so the `total market revenue` you divide by is
systematically too small. Every share is therefore systematically too large, and
because shares are squared, that tilt is amplified straight into the index. Your data
strategy and your model have drifted apart. An index that reads 2,862 and never
wobbles is not a correct index, only a confidently wrong one, and it can push a market
across the line competition authorities treat as highly concentrated. The fix is a
redesign of the data strategy, taking the denominator from a source built to cover
every seller, such as a government economic census, not one more year of the same
survey.

The block below computes the index both ways, with the survey's total and with the true one. Rerun it with different months and watch how little the wrong number moves.

```python
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
SEED = 464
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)

months = 12
chains = {"chain A": 38.5, "chain B": 29.5, "chain C": 21.0, "chain D": 13.5}
uncovered = 22.0     # independents + online delivery: real sales, never surveyed

avg = {c: rng.normal(rev, rev * 0.09, size=months).mean()
       for c, rev in chains.items()}
surveyed_total = sum(avg.values())

def index(total):
    return sum((rev / total * 100) ** 2 for rev in avg.values())

print(pd.DataFrame({"avg monthly revenue ($m)":
                    pd.Series(avg).round(1)}).to_string())
print(f"\nindex using the SURVEYED total : {index(surveyed_total):,.0f}")
print(f"index using the true total     : {index(surveyed_total + uncovered):,.0f}")
print("\naveraging twelve months bought precision, not correctness. the")
print("denominator is missing sales, so every share, and the index, tilts up")
```

## Mixed methods: two kinds of evidence, one question

Your concentration index says the grocery market is tight. A city councillor then asks a
different question: why do shoppers in some neighborhoods pay more for the same basket?
Shelf prices can tell you where the gap is and how large it is. They cannot tell you what
shoppers do about it, which store they would switch to, or whether they can reach another
store at all. For that you have to ask people.

**Mixed methods research** is a design that collects both numerical and qualitative
evidence (words, observations, and accounts rather than numbers) and joins them to
answer one question [@creswell2018designing]. Example: basket
prices recorded from store shelves, plus interviews with shoppers about where they buy
groceries and why. That makes it a hybrid design in exactly this chapter's sense: two
moving pieces, each with its own error, stitched into one answer. Everything the chapter
says about alignment applies. The price data and the interviews have to target the same
inquiry, or you end up with two studies sharing a cover page.

What separates a mixed-methods design from two studies stapled together is integration.
**Integration** means the planned points where you link the two kinds of evidence, so
that each one shapes how you read the other [@fetters2013achieving]. Fetters, Curry, and
Creswell locate it at three levels. At the design level you choose an order. An **explanatory sequence** is a design
where the numbers come first and interviews follow to explain them. Example: your prices
show a gap, so you interview shoppers in the neighborhoods where it is largest. An
**exploratory sequence** runs the other way, with interviews first and a measurement
built from what they reveal. Example: shoppers tell you they count the bus ride as part of
the price, so you add travel time to your basket. A **convergent design** collects both at
roughly the same time and compares them afterward. Example: you record shelf prices and
interview shoppers in the same month, then set the two side by side. At the methods
level, you choose how the two components touch. One can pick whom the other samples, as
when the price data choose which neighborhoods you visit (Fetters and colleagues call this
*connecting*). One can supply what the other measures, as the bus-ride remark did for your
basket (*building*). Or the two can be brought together only at analysis (*merging*), which
is what a convergent design does. At the interpretation and reporting level, you bring the
two together where a reader can inspect the meeting.

That last move has a tool. A **joint display** is a table or figure that puts the
numerical and the qualitative result for the same unit side by side, with a column that
says how they fit [@fetters2013achieving]. Example: one row per neighborhood, holding its
price gap, what its shoppers said about choice, and a verdict. Fetters and colleagues name
three kinds of fit. In *confirmation* the two agree. In *expansion* one covers an aspect of
the phenomenon the other cannot reach. In *discordance* they conflict. A discordant row often
teaches you the most, but it does not tell you which side is wrong. The numbers do not win
by default. The conflict may come from bias in either component, from a sampling choice,
or from two measures that were never tapping the same thing, and Fetters and colleagues
list the usual responses: look for the source of bias, re-analyze what you have, gather
more data, look to theory, or challenge whether your measures capture the construct you
named [@fetters2013achieving]. What you do not do is delete the row so the table reads
cleaner. If the conflict survives your checks, you report it.

The block below builds a small joint display. The prices are simulated and the interview
counts are constructed for the example. The block writes the rule for "fit" down before
it prints the table, which is the habit to copy: fix the rule first, so the table cannot
tempt you to bend it. Notice what a threshold rule cannot do. It sorts rows into agree and
conflict, but *expansion* needs a reading of what people actually said, so no cutoff will
assign it for you.

```python
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
SEED = 464
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)

# Six neighborhoods. The "price gap" is the basket price above the city median.
# The interview column is what you coded from 4 shopper interviews in each one.
hoods = ["Northgate", "Riverside", "Old Mill", "Eastfield", "Harbor", "Elm Park"]
chains = [1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 4]                     # chains within a 10-minute walk
gap = 9 - 2 * np.array(chains) + rng.normal(0, 1.5, size=6)
said_no_choice = [4, 3, 1, 3, 0, 0]              # interviewees who said "no other store"

jd = pd.DataFrame({"chains": chains, "price gap (%)": gap.round(1),
                   "said 'no other store' (of 4)": said_no_choice}, index=hoods)
def fit(row):
    high_gap, no_choice = row["price gap (%)"] > 3, row["said 'no other store' (of 4)"] >= 2
    if high_gap == no_choice:
        return "confirms"
    return "discordant: go back"
jd["fit"] = jd.apply(fit, axis=1)
print(jd.to_string())
print(f"\nrows that confirm   : {(jd['fit'] == 'confirms').sum()} of {len(jd)}")
print("\nagreement makes the description sturdier. it does not make the")
print("gap causal, and 4 interviews per place are not a prevalence estimate")
```

Four of the six rows confirm. Old Mill is the row to chase: its basket costs 6.5% more
than the city median, yet only one of four shoppers said they had no other store. Perhaps
they drive to a warehouse club outside your map, which would mean your count of chains
within a walk measures the wrong market. That is the alignment problem again, surfaced by
the discordance. Harbor sits at 3.8%, just over the 3% line you chose, with nobody
reporting a lack of choice. That row is a warning about your cutoff as much as about
Harbor.

Now the limit that matters most. Agreement between the two components creates no crossing
license. When prices and interviews both point at "one chain, no choice, higher prices",
the description is sturdier, because two methods with different weaknesses reached it.
That holds only if the weaknesses really are separate. If you coded the interviews while
looking at the price column, your reading of the quotes can bend toward the numbers, so
code them first, or have someone who has not seen the prices code them. The councillor's
question also stays what it was. "Why" is a causal question, and a joint display does not
turn it into a descriptive one. It gives you a sturdier description and a candidate
mechanism, while the causal answer stays unidentified for now. The claim that missing
competition *raises* prices still needs its own
identification argument. Both components can share a confounder: high rents could keep
competitors out of a neighborhood and push up every shelf price, and shoppers would
describe the same situation either way. Four interviews per neighborhood, chosen on
purpose rather than at random, also license no prevalence claim, meaning no claim about
how common a view is among all the neighborhood's shoppers. "Three of four" counts the people you chose
to hear, not a share of the neighborhood. Each component carries its own warrant into the
joint display, and the table cannot upgrade either one.

An AI tool helps here in bounded ways. It can draft an interview guide from your price
findings, lay out the joint display, and flag rows where your codes and your numbers
disagree. It fails in a predictable direction. Asked to "integrate the findings", it
writes a smooth narrative in which every quote supports every number, and the discordant
rows disappear. Which rows count as discordant, and what you go back to measure because of
them, stays your call. For the qualitative half on its own terms, including whom to
interview and how to trace every theme back to what people actually said, work through
[the further-route chapter on qualitative inquiry](../part7-further-routes/qualitative-inquiry.qmd).

## When the simulation is the research

So far in this chapter, simulation has been a check. You plant a known bias, as the
grocery block did with the missing stores, run the design, and see whether your answer
strategy finds it. Some projects turn that
around, and the simulated world becomes the thing you study. The economist Thomas
Schelling asked whether a city could end up sharply divided even if nobody wanted
division, only a mild wish not to be heavily outnumbered on their own block. He could not
rerun a city. So he built one out of rules and watched what the rules produced
[@schelling1971dynamic].

An **agent-based model** is a simulation in which many individual actors each follow
simple written rules, and the pattern you study emerges from their interactions. Example:
households on a grid, each moving to a random empty cell when fewer than 30% of its
neighbors are like it. A **process model** is the broader family: any simulation that
writes a mechanism down step by step. Example: a model of how an infection spreads through
a herd of cattle, or how a rumor moves through a firm's email network. In MIDA terms, the
Model is now your code, and the Inquiry is a quantity inside that code's world. The Data
strategy is which settings you run, with how many seeds, and what you record from each
run. The Answer strategy is how you summarize what comes out.

The distinction you must never blur is between two kinds of claim. A **model-world
claim** is a statement about what happens in the world your rules define. Example: "in
this model, a 30% preference produces heavy sorting." An **observed-world claim** is a
statement about what happened in a real place. Example: "this city is segregated because
of mild preferences." A simulation can settle the first, up to run-to-run wobble and only
at the settings you actually ran. It settles the second not at all. What it can support is a sufficiency claim: these rules
are enough to generate the pattern. Schelling drew the sharp consequence himself, that
inferences about individual motives usually cannot be drawn from aggregate patterns
[@schelling1971dynamic]. Many different rule sets, including deliberate exclusion, can
produce the same map.

The block below builds a small, simplified variant of the model. In Schelling's own
version an unhappy household moves to the nearest spot that would satisfy it; here it
jumps to a random empty cell, which is a different rule and can give a different number.
Read the three lines it prints before you read the moral.

```python
import numpy as np
SEED = 464
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)

N, EMPTY, WANT = 30, 0.10, 0.30   # 30x30 grid, 10% empty, each wants >= 30% alike

def like_share(g):
    """Average share of an agent's occupied neighbors that are its own type."""
    shares = []
    for i, j in zip(*np.nonzero(g)):
        nb = g[max(i-1, 0):i+2, max(j-1, 0):j+2].ravel()
        nb = nb[nb != 0]
        if len(nb) > 1:
            shares.append(((nb == g[i, j]).sum() - 1) / (len(nb) - 1))
    return np.mean(shares)

def unhappy(g):
    """How many agents still have fewer than WANT like neighbors."""
    count = 0
    for i, j in zip(*np.nonzero(g)):
        nb = g[max(i-1, 0):i+2, max(j-1, 0):j+2].ravel()
        nb = nb[nb != 0]
        count += len(nb) > 1 and ((nb == g[i, j]).sum() - 1) / (len(nb) - 1) < WANT
    return count

def run(rng, rounds=40):
    g = rng.choice([0, 1, 2], size=(N, N), p=[EMPTY, (1-EMPTY)/2, (1-EMPTY)/2])
    start, sizes = like_share(g), np.bincount(g.ravel(), minlength=3)
    for _ in range(rounds):
        cells = list(zip(*np.nonzero(g)))
        for k in rng.permutation(len(cells)):       # one agent at a time
            i, j = cells[k]
            nb = g[max(i-1, 0):i+2, max(j-1, 0):j+2].ravel()
            nb = nb[nb != 0]
            if len(nb) > 1 and ((nb == g[i, j]).sum() - 1) / (len(nb) - 1) < WANT:
                empties = list(zip(*np.nonzero(g == 0)))
                e = empties[rng.integers(len(empties))]
                g[e], g[i, j] = g[i, j], 0          # unhappy agent moves to a random empty cell
    kept = (np.bincount(g.ravel(), minlength=3) == sizes).all()   # nobody created or lost
    return start, like_share(g), unhappy(g), kept

results = np.array([run(rng) for _ in range(5)], dtype=float)
print(f"like-neighbor share at start : {results[:, 0].mean():.2f} "
      f"(runs {results[:, 0].min():.2f} to {results[:, 0].max():.2f})")
print(f"like-neighbor share at end   : {results[:, 1].mean():.2f} "
      f"(runs {results[:, 1].min():.2f} to {results[:, 1].max():.2f})")
print(f"code checks, every run : {int(results[:, 2].max())} still unhappy, "
      f"household counts kept = {bool(results[:, 3].all())}")
print("\nin THIS model world, asking for 30% alike ends near 76% alike.")
print("the rule is enough to make the pattern; no real city was observed")
```

With each household asking for only 30% like neighbors, the average share of like
neighbors climbs from 0.50 under random placement to 0.76, and the five runs end between
0.75 and 0.77. That narrow spread is the model's own variance across seeds, and it is the
only uncertainty five runs can measure. It says nothing about the choices you fixed: the
grid size, the share of empty cells, the move rule, the number of rounds. Changing those
and watching the end share is a sensitivity analysis, and a model-world claim reaches only
as far as the settings you swept. Nothing in the output measures how far the rules sit from
real households either. That distance is a systematic error, and, as with the grocery
survey's missing stores, more runs will never shrink it.

Two checks keep a simulation study honest, and they answer different questions
[@sargent2013verification]. **Verification** asks whether the code does what your written
model says. Example: the block's third line checks two things the written rules promise.
Moving must never create or delete a household, and if forty rounds were enough for the
city to settle, no one should be left below the 30% wish. In all five runs no one is left
unhappy and every count is kept. A
second test sets `WANT` to 0, so no one is ever unhappy. No one should move, and the end
share should equal the start share; it does, at 0.50. **Validation** asks whether the
model world resembles the observed world closely enough for the purpose you state.
Example: compare the model's clustering with block-level census maps of a real city.
Verification is about your code. Validation is always judged against a purpose, so a
model can pass for one question and fail for another. And even a close match earns only
the modest conclusion that the mechanism is consistent with the pattern, not that it
produced it.

A model is only as checkable as its description, so the field has a standard way to write
one down. The **ODD protocol** (Overview, Design concepts, Details) is a fixed template for
describing an agent-based model completely enough that someone else could rebuild it from
the text alone [@grimm2020odd]. Example: the Overview part includes a scheduling element
that states whether agents move one at a time or all at once, a choice the block above
makes in one line and one that can change the result. Ecologists use these models for animal movement, political scientists
for how opinions cluster, and business researchers for how buyers choose among sellers.

AI tools write agent-based code fast, and that speed is the risk. A tool asked to "make it
run faster" may switch from one-at-a-time moves to simultaneous moves, which is a
different model that can give a different answer, and report the new number as if nothing had
changed. If you let it, it will also describe a model-world result in observed-world
words. *AI is your arm and your research assistant, not your brain*: it can build the
city in seconds. Choosing the rules, deciding which real pattern would count as
validation, and writing the sentence that keeps the claim inside the model world stay
yours.

## An AI failure case

You paste your revenue table into an AI tool and ask for the concentration index. It
returns, with total confidence, `index = 2,862 ± 18`. The number looks plausible for a
market with a few big chains, the interval is tiny, and the code ran without an error.
It is wrong. The tool propagated only the *month-to-month* revenue variance, the part
you already crushed by averaging twelve months, and never modeled the *systematic* bias
from a denominator that leaves out every seller your survey does not reach. That tight
`± 18` describes wobble it could see and stays silent about the tilt it could not.

You catch it in two moves. First, check the assumption the number rests on: does the
total your shares divide by actually cover the whole market? Second, run a falsification
move: recompute the index from a deliberately narrower survey, dropping the smallest
chains too, and watch the "precise" index drift systematically upward. A quantity that
shifts well outside its own stated interval had an uncertainty that was never honest.
Verify the number, not the tidy interval beside it.

*You have studied your primary pathway and at least one useful contrast. This step decides whether your own project
needs more than one moving piece, and makes you justify the answer either way. The
four MIDA parts you are taking apart here are Blair, Cooper, Coppock, and Humphreys'
framework, developed at book length in RDSS.*

The hands-on half of this section lives in the chapter's **companion notebook**: open it in Colab with the badge at the top, and work the steps there.

Commit your own answer first, then delegate. Each prompt is a checkable job, not a
request for a verdict. Run them as a loop rather than a single shot: the second
pass, where you hand back the piece the tool skipped and ask again, is usually the
one that finds the uncharacterized step. Agentic tools that chain those passes
themselves will assemble a complete-looking error budget in one go. A complete look
is the failure mode this chapter is about.

::: {.callout-important title="Do not delegate"}
Three calls stay yours. You decide **what single quantity your inquiry names** (which
market, over what geography and time window), **whether each sub-design actually
targets that same quantity** so the parts align, and **whether to trust a combined number your diagnosis
says a systematic error dominates**. A tool can propagate the arithmetic, but it cannot
decide that a precise number is a correct one. That judgment is the whole point of the
chapter, and it is yours.
:::

1. Write your design as an ordered list of the measurements and stages it takes to
   get from raw data to your answer. One line means a simple design. Two or more
   means you are running a hybrid, whether you meant to or not.
2. For each line, name which MIDA part it lives in and the single quantity it
   targets. Then hold the list against your inquiry. Do all the pieces point at the
   same quantity, or has one quietly drifted to a neighboring one?

   **Decompose the design into pieces you can check.**

   ```text
   Here is my combined design: [paste your model, inquiry, and how you measure each
   seller's revenue and the total market revenue]. Break it into sub-designs. For each
   sub-measurement, name which MIDA part it lives in, the one assumption it depends on,
   and how its error enters the final index. Return a table.
   ```

   After running, verify: set the table beside your own decomposition. Any sub-design or
   assumption it skipped is exactly the gap to chase. Counters *illusion of completeness*
   (a tidy table that omits the one uncharacterized step).
3. Pick the piece whose error would hurt most and trace how its uncertainty reaches
   your final answer. Flag any step that squares, divides, or ratios a measured
   value, because a small tilt gets amplified exactly there.

   **Locate the real rule.**

   ```text
   Act as an industrial-organization research assistant. For a market concentration index
   computed as the sum of every seller's squared market share, name two things and cite a
   real, retrievable source for each: (1) the index thresholds competition authorities use
   to call a market moderately or highly concentrated, and (2) the standard rule for
   propagating the uncertainty in the measured revenues and the market total into the
   index. Only state values you are confident exist.
   ```

   After running, verify: open the cited source and confirm the thresholds and the
   propagation rule actually appear there. Counters *confident fabrication* (an invented
   threshold arrives as confidently as a real one).
4. Decide, and write the one-sentence justification. Either "this piece buys me
   something a single measurement cannot, and I can characterize its error," or
   "this piece adds a step I cannot characterize, so I am cutting it and narrowing
   my claim to match."
5. Name the systematic error in what remains that more data will never shrink, and
   what you would have to change instead: a different source, a wider sampling
   frame, a better instrument.

   **Red-team the combined result.**

   ```text
   Act as a hostile antitrust economist. Here is my measured concentration index and its
   stated uncertainty: [paste]. Name the single systematic error that more months of data
   can never fix and the place my four MIDA parts fail to point at the same quantity. Do
   not fix it for me.
   ```

   After running, verify: if it only praises your precision, push back and demand the one
   worst systematic error. Counters *sycophantic agreement* (praise that reviews your ego,
   not your error budget).
6. Log the step in your AI Research Ledger, and verify at least one output with a
   named method from the [Verification Guide](../verification-guide.qmd).
   Simulation is the natural check for a stitched design: plant a known bias in one
   piece, run the whole thing many times, and watch the variance shrink while the
   bias sits exactly where you put it. An AI reviewer may run the check with you;
   the decision to accept or reject stays yours.
